title: Spectator stream checkpointer and safe recapture protocol
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Problem: We continue to see rare but user-visible decode correctness regressions when CUDA graph capture/replay interleaves across multiple streams that observe shared KV/cache state. Root cause analysis indicates race windows during capture where spectator streams (streams that participate in kernel probing but do not own prefill transactions) can observe partial kernel state or in-flight kernel pointers. This leads to non-deterministic token outputs after replay and occasional OOMs when kernel occupancies are mispredicted.

Goal: Implement a spectator stream checkpointer and a safe-recapture protocol that: (1) snapshots minimal required stream-visible state in a lightweight checkpointer before capture, (2) expands the capture fencing to include spectator quiescence without serializing the entire prefill workload, and (3) provides deterministic replay fallback and correctness assertion hooks. Secondary goals: keep latency SLO impact < 3% for typical prefill sizes and limit throughput regression to < 5% on Dedicated GPU pools.

Technical approach summary:
- Introduce a per-stream "spectator checkpoint" structure capturing KV-cache epoch, prefix-hash, active kernel descriptor IDs, and a compact occupancy hint. Checkpoints are taken lock-free via atomic fences and cached in host memory.
- Extend kernel selection path to consult checkpoint-provided occupancy hints; for mismatches we probe in diagnostic mode (dry-run kernel launch with null outputs) to detect misbinds without altering GPU-visible state.
- Safe recapture protocol: when a capture would include spectator streams that are not quiescent, we perform a short quiesce window where only spectator checkpointer updates are allowed; if checkpointer drift detected, we trigger deterministic recapture flow: release the tentative CUDA graph, synchronize relevant streams, regenerate a fresh graph segment for the affected sequence, and swap atomically.
- Fallback policy: if deterministic recapture fails after N attempts (configurable, default 2), route the request to a compatible non-graph execution path and raise an SRE alert.

Acceptance criteria:
- Deterministic replay correctness for our internal fuzz harness (100k synthetic multi-client sequences) with zero mismatches compared to reference CPU decode.
- Perf: <3% median latency regression for prefill length 64 on p4d instances, <5% throughput decrease under 75th percentile load.
- No increased OOM incidence in production canary across 10k requests/day for 7 days.
- Feature guarded by config flag (runtime.graph.spectator_checkpoint=true) and rollout via canary cohort.

Out-of-scope: global graph serialization redesign, cross-node graph sharing, quantization-specific kernel rewriters.
implementation_notes: Key implementation pieces: checkpoint struct (host-only), light-weight probe kernel for occupancy validation, capture coordinator change to check checkpoint drift, atomic swap for graph segments. Keep allocation paths unchanged for existing fast path when guard disabled.
tests: (list) unit: checkpoint atomicity, simulated drift; integration: multi-stream capture/replay with fuzzer; perf: p4d perf suite for latency/throughput baselines; canary: 500-request cohort across dedicated cluster. Compare outputs to reference CPU decode harness and log any mismatch with token-level diff.
rollout_plan: Feature gated. Stage 1: internal canary (dev-only) for 48h. Stage 2: 1% customer canary for 7d with strict metrics (replay-mismatch rate, OOMs, latency). Stage 3: 25% then 100% if metrics stable. Auto-fallback to non-graph path on mismatch or if recapture fails >2 times.
risks: Extra quiesce windows might increase tail latency under certain burst shapes; probe kernel could add minimal kernel launches and perturb scheduling; complexity increases surface area for kernel-selector bugs. Mitigation: conservative defaults, canary rollout, and extensive fuzz tests.
alternative_considered: 1) Serialize entire prefill during capture — simple but unacceptable latency impact. 2) Aggressive kernel fingerprinting — lighter but brittle across quantized variants. 3) Per-request exclusive graphs — too costly for throughput. We chose checkpoint+recapture for best trade-off between correctness and perf.
